content: The Chokecherry, scientifically known as Prunus virginiana, is a species of bird cherry (Prunus subgenus Padus) that is native to North America. It is widely distributed across the continent, with the exception of the deep southern regions and the far northern areas. This plant typically grows as a suckering shrub or a small tree, reaching a height of approximately 5 meters. Its leaves are oval-shaped, measuring between 3 to 10 centimeters in length, and have coarsely serrated edges. The Chokecherry produces flowers in racemes containing 15 to 30 individual blooms, which appear in late spring, after the leaves have emerged. The fruit of the Chokecherry is small, about 1 centimeter in diameter, and bright red in color. The fruit has a highly astringent and sour taste. Similar to chokeberries, chokecherries are rich in antioxidant pigments, particularly anthocyanins. There are two recognized varieties of Chokecherry: 1. Common Chokecherry (Prunus virginiana var. virginiana): Found in eastern North America, this variety has leaves that are either hairless on the underside or have downy hairs only in the vein axils. 2. Western Chokecherry (Prunus virginiana var. demissa): Found in western North America, this variety has leaves that are downy on the underside. In the wild, Chokecherry is often regarded as a nuisance plant because it serves as a host for tent caterpillars, which can pose a threat to other fruit-bearing plants. However, certain cultivated varieties of Chokecherry, such as the 'Goertz' cultivar, are valued for their non-astringent and more palatable fruit. Research efforts, such as those conducted at the University of Saskatchewan, aim to develop new cultivars to enhance Chokecherry production and processing. Chokecherry is closely related to the Black Cherry (Prunus serotina), which is native to eastern North America. The two species can be distinguished by their size (Black Cherry can grow up to 30 meters tall), the size of their leaves, and the color of their ripe fruit (Chokecherry fruit is red, while Black Cherry fruit is black). The name chokecherry has also been used to refer to the related Manchurian Cherry or Amur Cherry (Prunus maackii), sometimes called Amur Chokecherry. Wilting causes the release of cyanide, which makes the plant sweeter and more palatable to horses. Ingesting 5 to 10 kilograms of Chokecherry foliage can be fatal to a horse. Symptoms of cyanide poisoning in horses include heavy breathing, agitation, and weakness. The leaves of the Chokecherry also serve as a food source for the caterpillars of various Lepidoptera species. For a detailed list of Lepidoptera that feed on Prunus species, refer to relevant entomological resources. It is worth mentioning that the chokeberries (Aronia genus) are often mistakenly referred to as chokecherries. This confusion is understandable, as there is a Chokecherry cultivar named Prunus virginiana 'Melanocarpa' and a chokeberry species named Aronia melanocarpa.
